title: tapi — but
pattern: A, tapi B · A. Tapi B.
explanation: tapi joins two ideas that pull against each other: Enak, tapi agak pedas. — It's good, but a bit spicy. A comma goes before it, and it can also start a new sentence: Tapi saya kangen keluarga. tetapi is the full form, used in writing and speeches; in conversation everyone says tapi. A very common pattern names a small problem, then waves it away: Agak jauh, tapi tidak apa-apa (casual: tapi nggak apa-apa) — it's a bit far, but that's fine.
natural: tapi is right in almost any conversation, polite or casual. The tapi tidak apa-apa pattern is a kind way to mention a problem without making a fuss.
stiff: tetapi in a chat sounds like reading aloud, and namun (however) belongs in writing and on the news.

examples.english: It's good, but a bit spicy.

gap.why: Something good, then a drawback: tapi.

examples.indonesian: Saya mau ikut, tapi saya harus kerja.
examples.english: I'd like to come, but I have to work.

gap.why: What you want and what stops you pull against each other: tapi.

examples.indonesian: Hotelnya agak jauh, tapi tidak apa-apa.
examples.english: The hotel's a bit far, but that's fine.

gap.why: tapi tidak apa-apa softens a problem: it's not ideal, but it's fine.

examples.indonesian: Saya suka tinggal di sini. Tapi saya kangen keluarga.
examples.english: I like living here. But I miss my family.

gap.note: Tetapi is the same word in full. It's correct, but in a chat like this it sounds written.
gap.why: Tapi can start a new sentence that pulls against the one before.
